page.title: How a cell works, one step at a time
page.description: Thirteen sections in four acts: copying DNA, using genes, proteins at work, energy and reading DNA. Each has an animated hero and live counts; most have a 'what if' branch.

sections.heading: Copying a ladder whose sides run opposite ways
text: The two strands of DNA run in opposite directions, but DNA polymerase can only build a new strand 5'→3'. Follow one replication fork to see how both strands still get copied at the same time, and why each daughter molecule keeps one old strand.

initial.caption: Parent DNA: every letter paired.
initial.note: Drawn flat, not to scale. Each new strand is marked with a "new" tag under it.

panels.title: Lagging template · Okazaki pieces
panels.label: old lower strand, 3'→5' left to right

steps.text: A parent DNA duplex. The two strands run in opposite directions: the upper reads 5'→3' left to right, the lower 3'→5'. The rule for every copy: DNA polymerase can only add a nucleotide to a free 3' end, so a new strand always grows 5'→3'.
steps.note: Illustrative 20-letter stretch of a much longer chromosome; drawn flat, not as a helix. Letters are not to scale.

fork.caption: Parent DNA: every letter paired, A with T and G with C.

lag.note: The lower parent strand, letter for letter as drawn in the scene.

steps.text: Helicase binds at a replication origin (off the right edge of this view) and moves left, breaking the base pairs ahead of it. The opened point is the replication fork. Both separated strands now act as templates.
steps.note: A real cell opens many origins at once, and forks move outward in both directions; one fork is shown.

fork.caption: Helicase opens letters 15–20; the lower strand drops away.

marks.label: single strand, exposed by the fork

steps.text: Polymerase cannot start a strand from nothing. Primase lays a short RNA primer on each template, and each primer supplies the free 3' end that polymerase needs.
steps.note: Primers are RNA; real primers are about 10 nucleotides long.

fork.caption: A primer pairs at 18–20 on the upper template.

marks.label: single strand, exposed by the fork

steps.text: DNA polymerase extends the upper template's primer. Its new strand grows 5'→3', which here is right to left: toward the fork, so it can follow the helicase without stopping. This is the leading strand. On the lower template, 5'→3' points away from the fork, so piece 1 grows to the right.
steps.note: In the scene, lower letters right of the polymerase are the new strand: same letters as the old lower strand. The old lower strand is the template in the lagging panel.

fork.caption: The fork reaches 8; new partners now pair with 15–20.

marks.label: single strand, exposed by the fork
piece 1 grows 5'→3', away from the fork

log.text: leading strand grows toward the fork
piece 1 grows away from the fork

steps.text: The fork moves on and the leading strand keeps pace in one continuous piece. The lagging template has exposed a fresh stretch near the fork, so a second primer is laid there and piece 2 grows right until it meets primer 1.

marks.label: single strand, exposed by the fork
piece 1 grows 5'→3', away from the fork

steps.text: The fork reaches the left edge of this view. A third primer and piece 3 complete the lagging copy here. Both strands are made at the same time, at the same fork; the lagging strand is just made in short pieces (Okazaki fragments).
steps.note: Pieces here are 6–7 letters. Real Okazaki fragments are roughly 100–200 nucleotides in eukaryotes and 1,000–2,000 in bacteria.

fork.caption: The fork has reached the left edge of this view; the molecule continues.

marks.label: piece 1 grows 5'→3', away from the fork

steps.text: The RNA primers are removed and replaced with DNA by another polymerase, which fills each gap by extending the 3' end of the neighbouring piece. What remains between neighbouring pieces is a nick: a break in one backbone where two letters sit side by side but are not bonded.

fork.caption: The primer is replaced with DNA; the leading strand is all DNA.

steps.note: Each primer is replaced by extending the piece that ends just before it, so the nick sits where that extension meets the next piece's first DNA letter. Primer 3 is replaced the same way by the next piece to the left, off this view.

steps.text: DNA ligase seals each nick by joining the backbone, so the three pieces become one continuous new strand.
steps.note: Ligase acts on the lagging template's new strand, shown in the right panel; the scene shows the leading side.

fork.caption: Leading side finished: one old strand paired with one new.

marks.label: one continuous new strand, sealed by ligase

steps.text: Two daughter duplexes now exist where there was one. Each has one old strand, used as the template, and one new strand. This is semi-conservative replication.

fork.caption: Daughter 1: old upper strand + new lower strand.

lag.note: Daughter 2: this old lower strand paired with its new, joined strand.

log.text: each daughter: one old strand, one new

steps.text: Before following the real mechanism, test a rival idea from the 1950s: the conservative model. In it, the parent duplex would come back together intact after copying, and the copy would be made of two brand-new strands. One daughter all old, one all new.
steps.note: Shown only as a prediction that was tested and rejected. No cell copies DNA this way.

labels.text: its copy would be new + new

fork.caption: Conservative model (rejected): the parent duplex would re-form.

lag.note: Prediction: this old strand would end up back with the old upper strand, never with a new partner.

steps.text: Meselson and Stahl (1958) grew bacteria with heavy nitrogen in their DNA, then let them copy it once in normal nitrogen. The conservative model predicts two bands, one heavy and one light. They found a single band of in-between density: every daughter was half old, half new. The conservative model was rejected; switch to the semi-conservative path to see how the copying works.
steps.note: Experiment summarised as textbooks report it; a second generation gave half-heavy and light bands, ruling out the dispersive model too.

fork.caption: Observed: one hybrid band, not the heavy + light pair predicted.

labels.text: density tube after one round of copying

sections.heading: Twice the DNA, the same chromosome count
text: Before a cell divides it copies every chromosome, so for a while it holds twice the DNA. Yet each daughter ends up with exactly the parent's number of chromosomes. Follow one cartoon cell with four chromosomes and watch the two counts in the table: chromosomes and DNA molecules.
The second path shows the G2/M checkpoint at work: if copying is not finished, the cell waits instead of dividing.

initial.caption: G1: four chromosomes in two pairs. M from mother, P from father.
initial.note: Cartoon cell, not to scale. Chromosomes drawn as pills (no X shapes or spindle); the nucleus stays drawn through mitosis. 2n = 4 is chosen for clarity; human cells have 2n = 46.
Count chromosomes by centromeres: one centromere, one chromosome.

steps.text: G1. This cartoon cell is diploid with 2n = 4: two pairs of chromosomes, one of each pair inherited from each parent. Each chromosome is a single DNA molecule, so the count is 4 chromosomes and 4 DNA molecules.

cell.caption: G1: four chromosomes, two pairs. M = from mother, P = from father.

steps.text: S phase. Zoom into the nucleus: every chromosome is replicated. Each copy is identical, so each chromosome now has two sister chromatids side by side, held together at a centromere. DNA molecules double from 4 to 8.

cell.caption: S: each chromosome now has a sister chromatid (′ marks the copy).

steps.text: Why is the chromosome count still 4? Two sister chromatids share one centromere and count as one chromosome. Copying doubled the DNA, not the number of chromosomes.

cell.caption: Count centromeres, not pills: still 4 chromosomes.

count.note: Same chromosome count, twice the DNA: one centromere per chromosome.

steps.text: G2. The view returns to the whole cell. The cell keeps growing and makes the proteins it needs to divide. The counts stay at 4 chromosomes and 8 DNA molecules.

cell.caption: G2: the copies wait inside the nucleus.

steps.text: The G2/M checkpoint. Control proteins check that every chromosome has been completely copied and that the DNA is not damaged. Here everything is complete, so the cell is allowed to enter mitosis.

cell.caption: Checkpoint: all four chromosomes fully copied, so mitosis can begin.

count.note: Checked: 4 chromosomes, each with 2 complete chromatids.

steps.text: Mitosis, metaphase. The chromosomes condense and line up one by one across the middle of the cell. Each sister chromatid faces the opposite side. In mitosis the two members of a pair do not join up; each lines up on its own.

cell.caption: Metaphase: four chromosomes in a single line.

steps.text: Anaphase. The sister chromatids of every chromosome separate and are pulled to opposite sides. Each separated chromatid now counts as a chromosome in its own right: 8 chromosomes and 8 DNA molecules, for a short time, in one cell.

cell.caption: Anaphase: sisters part; one full set moves to each side.

count.note: Each chromatid now has its own centromere, so 8 chromosomes.

steps.text: Telophase and cytokinesis. A nucleus forms around each set and the cytoplasm splits in two. Each daughter cell receives one copy of every chromosome: 1M, 1P, 2M and 2P.

cell.caption: Cytokinesis: two daughter cells, each with 1M, 1P, 2M, 2P.

steps.text: Two daughter cells in G1, each genetically identical to the parent and to each other: 4 chromosomes and 4 DNA molecules apiece. The DNA doubled once and was halved once, so the chromosome number is kept.

cell.caption: Both daughters start G1 with the parent's count.

count.note: Copy once (S), separate once (anaphase): the count is kept at 4.

steps.text: Another cell, same start. During S phase one stretch of chromosome 2P has not finished copying when the rest are done. Its sister chromatid, 2P′, is only partly made (drawn with ½), so it is not yet a whole DNA molecule.

cell.caption: S: seven copies done; 2P′ (½) is still being copied.

count.note: Simplified: replication is shown as finished or not for a whole copy.

steps.text: At the G2/M checkpoint the control proteins detect the unfinished copy. The signal to start mitosis is held back, so the cell does not divide.

cell.caption: Checkpoint: copying unfinished, so no mitosis yet.

count.note: Held: no chromatids separate while any copy is incomplete.

steps.text: The cell waits in G2 and the counts stay put: 4 chromosomes, one copy still unfinished. Only when copying is complete does the checkpoint let mitosis begin, so normally no daughter receives a half-copied chromosome.

cell.caption: G2 hold: same cell, same counts, no division.

count.note: Waiting protects the count: each daughter must get complete copies.

sections.heading: The gene stays; a copy appears
text: To use a gene, the cell does not send the DNA itself. RNA polymerase reads one strand of the gene and builds a new molecule, messenger RNA (mRNA), letter by letter. The DNA is unwound only briefly and closes up again unchanged.
Simplified: illustrative sequence, one polymerase drawn at a time, no splicing. Unrevealed mRNA letters are dimmed because they have not been made yet.

steps.text: A gene is a stretch of double-stranded DNA. The top strand (5'→3') is the coding strand; the bottom strand is the template. Just upstream sits the promoter, a short sequence where copying can begin.

dna.caption: A gene at rest: promoter and the first codons, every letter paired.
dna.note: Illustrative 40-letter sequence, drawn flat and not to scale. Real promoters and genes are much longer.

rna.note: No mRNA yet. The dimmed letters preview what will be made; they do not exist yet.

steps.text: RNA polymerase binds when it collides with the promoter. Helper proteins (not drawn) help it recognise this sequence; until then it drifts and bumps into DNA at random.

dna.caption: RNA polymerase binds at the promoter (boxed).

steps.text: The polymerase separates the two strands over a short stretch where copying starts, opening a bubble. Only this small part of the gene is unwound at any moment.

dna.caption: Zoomed in: a short bubble opens and the template (lower) is exposed.

steps.text: The polymerase reads the template strand and links matching RNA letters, adding each one to the RNA's 3' end. The first six letters, ACAAUG, match the coding strand with U in place of T.

dna.caption: Copied DNA 9–14 into RNA; the bubble moves right with the polymerase.
dna.note: The tag under the bubble shows the RNA made so far. In a real bubble about 8 RNA letters stay paired with the template; the rest trails away.

rna.note: 6 of 30 letters made. Dimmed letters do not exist yet.

steps.text: It moves right along the gene. Behind it the DNA strands pair back together, so the bubble travels with the polymerase. The mRNA now has 12 letters.

dna.caption: Behind the polymerase the two DNA strands pair up again.

rna.note: 12 of 30 letters made. Dimmed letters do not exist yet.

steps.text: Each new RNA letter pairs with the template letter it is copied from (A with T, U with A, G with C, C with G). That is why the mRNA reads like the coding strand. 18 letters made.

dna.caption: The template strand is read 3'→5'; the RNA grows 5'→3'.

rna.note: 18 of 30 letters made. Dimmed letters do not exist yet.

steps.text: The growing RNA peels away from the template as a single strand. The DNA it came from is unchanged and stays in place. 24 letters made.

dna.caption: Still the same DNA: nothing is removed from the gene.

rna.note: 24 of 30 letters made. Dimmed letters do not exist yet.

steps.text: The last six letters are added. The whole transcribed stretch is copied, including a few letters before the start codon and after the stop codon.

dna.caption: The polymerase reaches the end of the transcribed stretch.

rna.note: 30 of 30 letters made: the whole copy now exists.

steps.text: At the end of the gene the polymerase lets go. The finished mRNA is released and the DNA closes up, exactly as it was before.

dna.caption: The DNA re-pairs completely. The gene is still there, unchanged.
dna.note: How a polymerase recognises the end of a gene is not shown.

rna.note: Finished mRNA, 30 letters. A ribosome will read it from AUG to UGA.

steps.text: Compare the two: the mRNA has the coding strand's letters, with U wherever the DNA has T. It was made from the template strand, and only that one strand was read.

dna.caption: Coding strand ATG…TGA corresponds to mRNA AUG…UGA.
dna.note: The coding strand was not read. It simply has the same letters as the mRNA, with T where the mRNA has U.

rna.note: In plant and animal cells the RNA is also processed (splicing, cap, tail) before use. Omitted here.

steps.text: The gene is not used up. Another RNA polymerase binds at the same promoter and makes another identical copy. A busy gene is copied many times, by many polymerases at once.

dna.caption: A new polymerase binds: one gene, many mRNA copies.
dna.note: In a real cell several polymerases can copy the same gene at once, one behind another.

rna.note: Copy 1 is finished; copy 2 will have exactly the same 30 letters.

sections.heading: Three letters, one amino acid
text: A ribosome reads an mRNA in codons of three letters. Step through one short mRNA: the ribosome moves one codon per step, a tRNA brings the matching amino acid and the chain grows by one, until a stop codon releases it. The alternate path asks what would happen if reading began one letter late.

initial.caption: mRNA letters 1–24; the ribosome has not started.
initial.note: Illustrative 24-letter mRNA, the AUG-to-UGA stretch made in the transcription section. "Ribo" is the ribosome; caps are tRNAs, each labelled with the amino acid it carries; RF is the release factor. Simplified: one ribosome; E site and wobble pairing not shown.
One-letter codes: A Ala, C Cys, G Gly, H His, I Ile, L Leu, M Met, N Asn, P Pro, R Arg, V Val, W Trp; * = stop.

steps.text: **An mRNA is read three letters at a time.** Each group of three, a codon, stands for one amino acid or for stop. Four letters in threes give 64 codons: 61 code for the 20 amino acids and 3 mean stop. Any stretch of letters could be split into threes in three different ways, so all three frames are shown.

log.text: 8 codons to read · chain: none yet

ribo.caption: Read in threes: 8 codons from AUG to UGA.

steps.text: **The start codon fixes the frame.** The small ribosomal subunit, carrying the initiator tRNA with methionine, binds near the 5' end and, in eukaryotes, moves along until the tRNA pairs with the first AUG. The large subunit joins. From here the ribosome reads frame 1 only, so the other two frames dim.

ribo.caption: Start: initiator tRNA-Met pairs with AUG in the P site.

steps.text: **Codon 2: GCC, alanine.** tRNAs carrying amino acids collide with the ribosome at random; only one whose anticodon (3'-CGG-5') pairs with GCC stays in the A site. The ribosome then joins methionine to alanine with a peptide bond, so the chain now hangs from the tRNA in the A site.

ribo.caption: Codon 2 in the A site; the chain is now on the Ala tRNA.

steps.text: **Codon 3: AUU, isoleucine.** The ribosome moves along the mRNA by exactly three letters. The empty tRNA leaves (through a third site, not shown), the tRNA holding the chain sits in the P site, and AUU is now in the A site, where a tRNA carrying isoleucine binds.

ribo.caption: Codon 3 in the A site; the chain is now on the Ile tRNA.

steps.text: **Codon 4: GUA, valine.** The same cycle repeats for every codon: matching tRNA binds, peptide bond, move three letters. The chain grows one amino acid at a time from its first end (the N-terminus).

ribo.caption: Codon 4 in the A site; the chain is now on the Val tRNA.

steps.text: **Codon 5: AUG again, methionine.** An AUG inside the gene just codes for methionine. Only the first AUG, where the ribosome began, sets the frame.

ribo.caption: Codon 5 in the A site; the chain is now on the Met tRNA.

steps.text: **Codon 6: GGC, glycine.** In a real cell this cycle runs at about 2 to 20 amino acids per second (fastest in bacteria), and many ribosomes can read the same mRNA at once.

ribo.caption: Codon 6 in the A site; the chain is now on the Gly tRNA.

steps.text: **Codon 7: CGC, arginine.** Seven codons read, seven amino acids joined. The next three letters are UGA.

ribo.caption: Codon 7 in the A site; the chain is now on the Arg tRNA.

steps.text: **UGA is a stop codon: no tRNA matches it.** A release factor, a protein shaped like a tRNA, binds in the A site instead. The bond holding the chain to the last tRNA is broken, the finished chain of seven amino acids is released, and the ribosome subunits separate from the mRNA.

ribo.caption: UGA: a release factor binds; the chain is released.
ribo.note: 24 letters = 7 codons + 1 stop codon, so 7 amino acids. Real proteins are usually hundreds of amino acids long.

steps.text: **Thought experiment: start one letter late.** Suppose reading began at letter 2 instead of at the AUG. The letters are the same, but every group of three is different: that is row F2. The first codon is now UGG, tryptophan. A normal ribosome does not do this; the thought experiment shows why the start codon matters.

ribo.caption: Thought experiment: reading from letter 2.
ribo.note: Thought experiment: a normal ribosome starts at the AUG. Row F2 of the frames panel is the shifted reading.

steps.text: **Every codon changes.** The next shifted codons are CCA, proline, and UUG, leucine. Compare the rows: from the start codon (F1) the chain begins Met-Ala-Ile; shifted by one letter (F2) it begins Trp-Pro-Leu. Not one amino acid is the same.

ribo.caption: Shifted codons: UGG, CCA, UUG. Every amino acid changes.

steps.text: **A stop codon arrives early.** The fourth shifted codon is UAA, a stop, so a release factor ends the chain after three amino acids that have nothing in common with the real protein. Starting at the right AUG is what keeps every later codon in step.

ribo.caption: Shifted codon 4 is UAA, a stop: the wrong chain ends early.

sections.heading: From gene to the cell surface
text: Cells export proteins such as digestive enzymes, antibodies and hormones like insulin. Follow one secreted protein from its gene to the outside of the cell: the mRNA leaves the nucleus, a ribosome on the rough ER makes the protein, and two rounds of vesicles carry it through the Golgi to the plasma membrane.
Cartoon cell, not to scale. A real cell runs thousands of copies of this pathway at once; here we follow one batch.

initial.caption: The gene's mRNA copy is ready in the nucleus.

steps.text: The gene for a secreted protein is in the nucleus. It has been copied into mRNA; the DNA itself never leaves.

cell.caption: The gene's mRNA copy is ready in the nucleus.
cell.note: Cartoon cell, not to scale. Splicing and the mRNA cap and tail are omitted.

steps.text: The mRNA leaves through a nuclear pore into the cytosol. Translation happens in the cytosol, not in the nucleus.

cell.caption: The mRNA crosses the nuclear envelope at a pore.
cell.note: Cartoon cell, not to scale. Pores are drawn as a single crossing point.

log.text: mRNA exported through a nuclear pore

steps.text: A free ribosome binds when it collides with the mRNA and starts translating. The first amino acids form a signal sequence: an address tag for the ER.

cell.caption: Translation begins in the cytosol; the signal sequence emerges first.
cell.note: Motion in the cytosol is random; the ribosome meets the mRNA by chance.

steps.text: A signal recognition particle (SRP) binds the signal sequence as it emerges. Translation pauses while SRP holds the ribosome.

cell.caption: SRP grabs the signal sequence; translation pauses.
cell.note: SRP is a particle made of RNA and protein.

steps.text: SRP binds its receptor on the ER membrane, docking the ribosome there. SRP then lets go and is reused; ribosomes on the ER are why it is called rough ER.

cell.caption: Docked on the rough ER; SRP is released.
cell.note: The ER is drawn as one sac; in a real cell it is a network of membranes joined to the nuclear envelope.

log.text: ribosome docked on the rough ER

steps.text: Translation resumes. The growing chain is threaded through a channel into the ER interior, and an enzyme cuts off the signal sequence.

cell.caption: The chain enters the ER interior through a channel.
cell.note: The chain enters through a protein channel in the ER membrane (not drawn).

log.text: chain threaded into the ER; signal sequence removed

steps.text: Inside the ER the protein folds, helped by chaperone proteins, and gains short sugar chains. Many ribosomes read the same mRNA, so copies build up.

cell.caption: Four folded copies wait in the ER interior.
cell.note: Count illustrative. Proteins that fail to fold are held back and broken down.

steps.text: Translation is finished, so the ribosome lets go of the ER. A patch of ER membrane buds off around the proteins, forming a transport vesicle that carries them to the Golgi.

cell.caption: An ER vesicle buds and moves toward the Golgi.
cell.note: Vesicles are membrane bubbles; the cargo never touches the cytosol.

steps.text: The vesicle fuses with the Golgi and empties its cargo inside. The Golgi trims and adds sugars and sorts proteins by destination.

cell.caption: Fused with the Golgi: sugars modified, cargo sorted.
cell.note: The Golgi is a stack of flattened sacs, drawn here as one.

log.text: vesicle fused; sugars modified, sorted for export

steps.text: A secretory vesicle buds from the far side of the Golgi with the finished proteins inside.

cell.caption: A secretory vesicle leaves the Golgi.
cell.note: Some cells store these vesicles until a signal triggers release (insulin works this way).

log.text: secretory vesicle budded from the Golgi

steps.text: Motor proteins carry the vesicle along the cytoskeleton to the plasma membrane. This step is directed, not random.

cell.caption: The vesicle reaches the plasma membrane.
cell.note: Cytoskeleton tracks and motor proteins are not drawn.

steps.text: Exocytosis: the vesicle membrane fuses with the plasma membrane and the proteins are released outside. The vesicle's membrane becomes part of the cell surface.

cell.caption: Exocytosis: the proteins are now outside the cell.
cell.note: Fusion needs membrane proteins that pull the two membranes together; not drawn.

steps.text: The whole route: nucleus to cytosol, rough ER, Golgi, vesicle, outside. Once inside the ER the protein never crosses another membrane: it rides inside membrane bubbles, and the last fusion opens one to the outside.

cell.caption: The standard route for proteins a cell secretes.
cell.note: Thousands of copies run in parallel in a real cell. A few proteins leave by other routes, not shown.

sections.heading: The switch is a protein letting go
text: Bacteria such as E. coli make the enzymes for using lactose only when lactose is present. The switch is a repressor protein. While it sits on a stretch of DNA called the operator, RNA polymerase cannot copy the genes. A form of lactose called allolactose binds the repressor and changes its shape, so it lets go, and the genes are copied into mRNA.

Follow the lactose path, or the no-lactose path where the repressor stays bound. In both paths the DNA letters never change. Simplified: control by glucose through the CAP protein is left out, and the sequence is illustrative.

panels.title: Strand scene · the lac operon switch
panels.label: E. coli DNA · start of the lac operon

initial.caption: No lactose: the repressor sits on the operator.
initial.note: Illustrative 28-letter sequence, not to scale: the real promoter and operator are longer and partly overlap. The upper strand reads 5'→3' left to right.
Dimmed letters have not been made yet. The mRNA matches the upper (coding) strand, with U in place of T.

steps.text: **Meet the switch.** A bacterium's genes for using lactose sit side by side, after one promoter and one operator. With no lactose around, a repressor protein is bound to the operator.

lac.caption: No lactose: the repressor sits on the operator.
lac.note: Illustrative 28-letter sequence, not to scale: the real promoter and operator are longer and partly overlap. The upper strand reads 5'→3' left to right.

steps.text: **RNA polymerase binds the promoter.** It reaches the promoter by random collisions and grips it. The promoter is where copying of this gene starts.

lac.caption: RNA polymerase binds when it collides with the promoter.
lac.note: A cell holds thousands of polymerase molecules moving at random; one of them binds here.

steps.text: **The repressor is in the way.** With the repressor on the operator, the polymerase cannot start copying the genes. Only an occasional transcript slips through.

lac.caption: Blocked: the bound repressor stops transcription starting.
lac.note: The genes are intact; only access to them is blocked. The rare transcript that slips through keeps a few enzyme molecules in the cell. Textbooks describe the block two ways (the repressor stops the polymerase binding, or stops it starting); either way almost no mRNA is made.

steps.text: **Lactose arrives.** Lactose enters through the few permease molecules already present. The few β-galactosidase molecules turn a little of it into allolactose, the molecule that acts as the signal.

lac.caption: Allolactose, made from lactose, moves about the cell.
lac.note: Textbooks often say "lactose binds the repressor"; strictly it is allolactose, a rearranged form of lactose.

steps.text: **Allolactose binds the repressor.** When it collides with the repressor it fits a pocket and binds. Binding changes the repressor's shape.

lac.caption: Allolactose binds the repressor; the repressor changes shape.
lac.note: Cartoon: allolactose binds the repressor protein, not the DNA. The real repressor works as a group of four protein chains.

steps.text: **The repressor lets go.** In its new shape the repressor no longer grips the operator. It falls off, carrying the allolactose with it. The DNA itself has not changed.

lac.caption: The repressor releases: the operator is free.
lac.note: No letters were added, removed or changed. The switch is a protein binding and letting go.

steps.text: **Transcription starts.** The polymerase opens a short stretch of the double helix and starts making mRNA, using the lower strand as the template.

lac.caption: The polymerase opens the helix and starts the mRNA.
lac.note: The opened stretch is the transcription bubble. The mRNA grows 5'→3', copying the lower (template) strand.

steps.text: **The polymerase moves along the gene.** The bubble moves with it: the DNA opens ahead and closes again behind. The mRNA gets longer, one letter at a time.

lac.caption: The bubble moves along; the DNA closes behind it.
lac.note: Behind the polymerase the two DNA strands pair up again. The mRNA leaves as a separate strand (not drawn on the DNA).

steps.text: **Through the first gene.** The polymerase copies lacZ and then the next two genes, lacY and lacA, into one long mRNA. Only its first letters are shown here.

lac.caption: It copies on past the view: lacZ, lacY, lacA in one mRNA.
lac.note: The full mRNA is several thousand letters long. Ribosomes start making the enzymes while it is still being made.

steps.text: **Lactose runs out, and the switch resets.** When the allolactose is used up, the repressor returns to its gripping shape. It binds the operator again, and transcription stops. The mRNA already made breaks down within minutes.

lac.caption: Allolactose used up: the repressor binds the operator again.
lac.note: The switch is reversible and depends on how much allolactose is present. Simplified: glucose control by the CAP protein is omitted.

labels.text: RNA pol has left the gene

mrna.note: The mRNA made earlier is broken down within minutes; no new copies are being made.

steps.text: **No lactose: nothing comes to free the operator.** Without allolactose the repressor stays in its gripping shape, and the polymerase stays stuck at the promoter.

lac.caption: No allolactose: the repressor stays bound.
lac.note: Repressor molecules do let go briefly from time to time, but they rebind almost at once, so almost no mRNA is made.

steps.text: **The genes stay silent.** The cell does not spend energy making lactose-using enzymes when there is no lactose. The DNA is the same as in the lactose case; only the protein on it differs.

labels.text: RNA pol has left the gene

lac.caption: The polymerase leaves; the genes stay off.
lac.note: Compare with the lactose path: same DNA, same polymerase. Only whether the repressor is bound decides the outcome. CAP and glucose control are omitted.

mrna.note: No mRNA: every letter stays dimmed because none has been made.

sections.heading: The enzyme is still there
text: An enzyme is a protein that speeds up one chemical reaction. A substrate molecule binds its active site, is converted to product, and the product leaves. The enzyme comes out unchanged, so one enzyme molecule can convert substrate after substrate. Follow one enzyme through two full cycles, then see what heat does to it.
bullets: Teaching cartoon of a generic enzyme: one substrate becomes one product here (many real reactions make two). Positions and counts are authored, not simulated.
The rate-by-temperature row is illustrative, shaped like a typical human enzyme with an optimum near 37 °C.
Alternate path: too hot. The enzyme's shape is lost and substrate no longer binds.

panels.title: One enzyme in solution
panels.label: one enzyme in solution · not to scale

panels.title: Relative rate by temperature (1.0 = peak, illustrative)

steps.text: One enzyme and six substrate molecules drift in solution. Nothing has reacted yet.

scene.caption: 1 enzyme · 6 substrate · 0 product
scene.note: Molecules move at random; they meet by collision. Teaching cartoon, not to scale.

steps.text: A substrate collides with the enzyme in the right orientation and binds its active site: the enzyme-substrate (ES) complex.

scene.caption: Cycle 1 · ES complex · 5 substrate left
scene.note: The active site fits only this substrate; binding can tighten the fit (induced fit), which this cartoon does not draw.

steps.text: Bonds rearrange inside the active site and the substrate becomes product, still held by the enzyme (EP).

scene.caption: Cycle 1 · EP complex · substrate converted
scene.note: The enzyme lowers the activation energy, so the reaction runs far faster. It does not change which way the reaction can go.

steps.text: The product leaves. The enzyme is free again, with the same shape and the same active site it started with.

scene.caption: 1 enzyme · 5 substrate · 1 product
scene.note: The product is held only weakly by the active site, so it soon drifts away.

steps.text: The same enzyme binds a second substrate molecule. Nothing about it was used up in the first cycle.

scene.caption: Cycle 2 · ES complex · 4 substrate left
scene.note: Same enzyme molecule, second substrate molecule. Nothing in the enzyme was consumed.

steps.text: Catalysis again: the second substrate is converted to product inside the active site.

scene.caption: Cycle 2 · EP complex · substrate converted
scene.note: Each cycle is the same chemistry: bind, convert, release.

steps.text: The second product leaves. Two substrates have become two products, and there is still exactly one enzyme.

scene.caption: 1 enzyme · 4 substrate · 2 product
scene.note: Enzymes are catalysts: they take part in the reaction but come out unchanged.

steps.text: The cycle repeats until the substrate runs out. Real enzymes turn over anywhere from less than one to millions of substrates per second, and a cell holds many copies of each enzyme.

scene.caption: 1 enzyme · 0 substrate · 6 product
scene.note: Four more cycles are skipped here; each one is the same bind, convert, release.

steps.text: Temperature changes the rate. Warmer means more frequent, faster collisions, so the rate climbs to an optimum (near 37 °C for many human enzymes). Hotter still, the enzyme starts to lose its shape and the rate falls.

scene.caption: 37 °C: frequent collisions and an intact active site, the fastest rate.
scene.note: Grid values are illustrative, shaped like a typical human enzyme. Other enzymes have other optima.

steps.text: Too hot: at 60 °C the weak bonds that hold the enzyme folded break. The chain of amino acids is still there, but its shape and the active site are lost. This is denaturation.

scene.caption: 60 °C · enzyme denatured · 6 substrate
scene.note: Denaturation unfolds the protein (drawn as a shapeless block, no active site); it does not break the amino-acid chain.

steps.text: A substrate still collides with the enzyme, but the active site no longer fits it, so it does not bind.

scene.caption: Collision, no ES complex
scene.note: Collisions still happen; without the right shape they produce no ES complex.

steps.text: No substrate binds, so no product forms: the rate is zero. Cooling down usually does not refold the enzyme, so the loss is often permanent.

scene.caption: 1 enzyme (denatured) · 6 substrate · 0 product
scene.note: Some proteins can refold after mild heating, but most enzymes heated this far do not.

sections.heading: Three out, two in, one ATP
text: Ions cannot cross the oily middle of a membrane on their own. A channel lets an ion move down its gradient for free (passive transport). The Na⁺/K⁺ pump moves ions up their gradients and pays with ATP (active transport): each cycle sends 3 Na⁺ out and brings 2 K⁺ in.
Step through one channel crossing, then two full pump cycles. Simplified cartoon: one pump and one channel stand for thousands, and dot counts are illustrative.

panels.title: Cell scene · a patch of cell membrane
panels.label: plasma membrane, close up

initial.caption: Na⁺ is crowded outside; K⁺ is crowded inside.

panels.title: Pump ledger · ions moved, ATP used

initial.note: net + out = 3 Na⁺ out − 2 K⁺ in: one positive charge leaves per cycle.

steps.text: Two gradients sit across one membrane. Na⁺ is about ten times more concentrated outside the cell; K⁺ is about thirty times more concentrated inside.

mem.caption: Na⁺ (cyan) crowded outside; K⁺ (white) crowded inside.
mem.note: Cartoon: dot counts are illustrative, not to scale. Concentrations are typical textbook values for a mammalian cell.

steps.text: Passive transport first. A K⁺ channel is an open pore: when a K⁺ ion collides with it, it can pass through, and more K⁺ crosses outward than inward because more is inside. No ATP is used.

mem.caption: Down its gradient, through a channel: no energy input.
mem.note: Real ions move randomly; the net flow is outward. One ion stands for many.

steps.text: Left alone, leaks like this would slowly run both gradients down. The Na⁺/K⁺ pump works the other way. Open to the inside, it binds 3 Na⁺ from the cytoplasm.

mem.caption: Three Na⁺ sites on the inner face are filled.
mem.note: A cell runs many pumps at once; one is drawn.

steps.text: With Na⁺ bound, ATP's end phosphate is transferred onto the pump itself. ADP is released; the phosphate stays attached to the pump for now.

mem.caption: ATP → ADP; the pump now carries a phosphate (P).

steps.text: Phosphorylation powers a shape change: the pump closes to the inside and opens to the outside. In this shape it holds Na⁺ weakly, so the 3 Na⁺ are released outside, against their gradient.

mem.caption: Pump faces out; 3 Na⁺ leave into the crowd outside.
mem.note: The pump is drawn in two shapes: a ring open to the inside, and a dome while it faces the outside.

steps.text: The outward-facing shape binds K⁺ strongly. When 2 K⁺ from outside collide with it and bind, the phosphate is released from the pump.

mem.caption: 2 K⁺ bound on the outer face; phosphate (Pi) released.

steps.text: Losing the phosphate returns the pump to its inward-facing shape, which holds K⁺ weakly. The 2 K⁺ are released into the cytoplasm. One cycle: 3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in, 1 ATP, so one net positive charge leaves.

mem.caption: Back to the start shape; 2 K⁺ delivered inside. ADP and Pi drift off.

steps.text: The cycle repeats as long as ATP is available. The pump is open inside again, 3 more Na⁺ bind, and a fresh ATP phosphorylates it.

mem.caption: Cycle 2: 3 Na⁺ bound, phosphate added from a new ATP.
mem.note: The cell keeps remaking ATP from ADP + Pi elsewhere (respiration); that is not drawn here.

steps.text: Again the pump flips to face out and releases 3 Na⁺ outside. 2 K⁺ bind, and the phosphate comes off.

mem.caption: 3 Na⁺ out; 2 K⁺ bound on the outer face.

steps.text: The pump faces in and releases the 2 K⁺. After two cycles: 6 Na⁺ out, 4 K⁺ in, 2 ATP used. Each cycle pushes one net positive charge out.

mem.caption: Two cycles done: both gradients are steeper.

steps.text: The gradients are stored energy, like water behind a dam: Na⁺ is pushed inward, and K⁺ leaks out through open channels. That K⁺ leak sets most of the resting voltage; the pump's own charge imbalance adds only a few millivolts. A nerve impulse spends these gradients next.

mem.caption: Gradients built by ATP, ready to be spent.
mem.note: Simplified. The pump uses a large share of a typical animal cell's ATP (textbook estimate: about a third).

sections.heading: Draw the spike
bullets: Step through one patch of axon membrane and watch the voltage trace draw a nerve impulse (an action potential): Na⁺ in, then K⁺ out.
The large trace is the membrane voltage, inside versus outside. The dashed amber line is the −55 mV threshold; above 0 mV the inside is positive.
Simplified: one cartoon patch, ion dots are symbolic, and values and timing are typical textbook approximations (a real spike lasts about 1–2 ms).

screens.label: rest
screens.alt: Flat line at minus 70 millivolts: the resting potential.

screens.label: threshold
screens.alt: The trace rises to the minus 55 millivolt threshold.

screens.label: peak
screens.alt: The trace shoots up to a peak of plus 30 millivolts.

screens.label: falling
screens.alt: The trace falls back through minus 20 millivolts.

screens.label: undershoot
screens.alt: The trace dips below rest to about minus 80 millivolts.

screens.label: one way
screens.alt: The trace recovers to about minus 74 millivolts: refractory.

screens.label: ready
screens.alt: The trace is back at minus 70 millivolts, the whole spike drawn.

screens.label: weak
screens.alt: A small bump to minus 60 millivolts, short of the dashed threshold.

screens.label: no spike
screens.alt: The bump fades back to minus 70 millivolts: no spike.

panels.title: Cell scene · a patch of axon membrane
panels.label: a patch of axon (cartoon)

initial.caption: At rest: Na⁺ is high outside, K⁺ is high inside.

steps.text: At rest the inside of the axon sits about 70 mV negative to the outside. The pump has built the gradients (more Na⁺ outside, more K⁺ inside), and a little K⁺ leaks out through always-open channels, which holds the charge here.
A stimulus (current spreading from an active neighbour or a synapse) makes the inside less negative. At about −55 mV, the threshold, voltage-gated Na⁺ channels begin to open.

mem.caption: Threshold reached: voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open.

steps.text: Na⁺ flows in through the open channels, down its concentration gradient and toward the negative inside. Each bit of entry depolarises the membrane further and opens more Na⁺ channels, so the inside swings positive, peaking near +30 mV.

mem.caption: Na⁺ rushes in, yet only a tiny fraction of the ions cross.

steps.text: Within about a millisecond the Na⁺ channels inactivate and stop letting Na⁺ through. Slower voltage-gated K⁺ channels are now open, K⁺ flows out, and the inside turns negative again. This K⁺ exit, not the pump, is what brings the voltage down.

mem.caption: Na⁺ channels inactivate; K⁺ flows out.

steps.text: The K⁺ channels are slow to close, so for a moment more K⁺ leaves than at rest and the membrane dips below rest, to about −80 mV: the undershoot.

mem.caption: K⁺ channels close slowly: a brief dip below rest.

steps.text: The positive charge that entered spreads along the inside and brings the patch ahead to threshold, so it fires in turn. This patch, now behind the impulse, cannot fire again yet: its Na⁺ channels are still recovering from inactivation (the refractory period). So the impulse travels one way.

mem.caption: Patch ahead fires; this patch is refractory.

log.text: patch ahead fires; this patch refractory

steps.text: This patch settles back to −70 mV, ready to fire again. Look at the ion counts: they barely changed, because a spike moves only a tiny fraction of the ions. The Na⁺/K⁺ pump keeps topping up the gradients over many spikes; it is not what repolarised the membrane.

mem.caption: Back at rest; ion counts barely changed.

steps.text: What if the stimulus is too weak? It nudges the inside up to about −60 mV, short of the −55 mV threshold. Too few Na⁺ channels open to start the positive feedback.

mem.caption: −60 mV: below threshold; most Na⁺ channels stay shut.

steps.text: The small change fades and the membrane drifts back to −70 mV. No spike: an action potential is all-or-none. A stronger stimulus does not make a bigger spike; it makes spikes come more often.

sections.heading: A hundred million answers
text: A hormone such as adrenaline never enters the cell it signals. It binds a receptor on the outside, and a relay of proteins inside passes the message on, multiplying it at each stage, until one molecule outside has released about a hundred million glucose units (textbook estimate). Then the relay switches itself off. Steroid hormones are the contrast case: they cross the membrane and act on genes in the nucleus.
bullets: **Simplified:** a cartoon liver cell, not to scale. Positions and dot counts are drawn, not simulated; a real cell holds many copies of every protein, and molecules meet by random collision.
**Amplification numbers** are the order-of-magnitude textbook example (after Campbell Biology's adrenaline and liver cell figure), shown as powers of ten.
**Steroid path:** cortisol stands for steroid-type signals in general; the drawing omits the DNA and the new proteins.

panels.title: Cell scene · a liver cell answers adrenaline
panels.label: cartoon liver cell, not to scale

initial.caption: At rest: adrenaline outside, every relay protein switched off.

steps.text: A liver cell at rest. **Adrenaline** (epinephrine) is carried in the blood outside. Inside, the relay proteins are all switched off, and glucose is stored as **glycogen**.
Adrenaline binds when it collides with the **receptor's outer face**. It *never enters* the cell: binding changes the receptor's shape, and that shape change is the message passed inward.

cell.caption: Bound on the outside; nothing crosses the membrane.

steps.text: The changed receptor makes a **G protein** on the inner face let go of GDP and pick up **GTP**, which switches it on. One bound receptor can switch on many G proteins before the hormone leaves.

cell.caption: G protein swaps GDP for GTP: switched on.

steps.text: The active G protein switches on **adenylyl cyclase**, an enzyme in the membrane. Each cyclase turns ATP into **cyclic AMP (cAMP)** again and again: one becomes 20 here.

cell.caption: Adenylyl cyclase on: ATP becomes cAMP, 20 so far.

steps.text: cAMP is the **second messenger**: small and soluble, it spreads through the cytoplasm. Where it collides with **protein kinase A (PKA)** it binds and switches the kinase on. The scene stops at 50 dots; the textbook figure is about 10⁴.

cell.caption: cAMP ×50 (drawn); PKA switched on.

steps.text: The **kinase tiers**. PKA adds phosphate groups to *phosphorylase kinase*, which in turn phosphorylates **glycogen phosphorylase**. Each active kinase modifies many copies of the next protein, so every tier multiplies the signal. (The middle tier, phosphorylase kinase, is not drawn.)

cell.caption: Phosphorylase switched on at the glycogen store.

steps.text: **The response.** Active phosphorylase cuts glucose units off glycogen (as glucose-1-phosphate, which the liver converts to glucose), and glucose leaves for the blood. Textbook estimate: about 10⁸ glucose units from **one** adrenaline molecule.

cell.caption: Glycogen broken down; glucose ×24 (drawn) leaves the cell.

steps.text: **Switching off is built in.** The G protein slowly cuts its own GTP to GDP and goes quiet, so the cyclase stops. Adrenaline lets go of the receptor. Enzymes called *phosphodiesterases* break down the cAMP that is left: 50 falls to 20.

cell.caption: GTP → GDP; cyclase off; cAMP falling (×20).

steps.text: The last cAMP is cleared and *phosphatases* remove the added phosphates, so the kinases and phosphorylase switch off and glycogen breakdown stops. The cell is back at rest, ready for the next knock: the answer lasts only while the hormone keeps arriving.

cell.caption: Back at rest. The released glucose stays in the blood.

steps.text: **A different kind of signal.** Cortisol is a *steroid* hormone: made from cholesterol, it dissolves in the membrane's lipid, so it passes straight through. The surface receptor and the G protein take no part.

cell.caption: Cortisol crosses the membrane; the surface relay stays off.

steps.text: Inside, cortisol binds when it collides with its own receptor protein, which waits in the cytoplasm. Binding changes the receptor's shape and frees it to move.

cell.caption: Cortisol bound to its receptor inside the cell.

steps.text: Zoomed in: the hormone–receptor pair moves into the **nucleus** through the nuclear pores. Here the signal itself reaches the DNA, something a surface signal like adrenaline never does.

cell.caption: Zoomed to the nucleus: the pair is inside.

steps.text: Inside the nucleus the pair binds DNA beside its target genes and switches their **transcription** on. New mRNA (white dots) is made; it will leave the nucleus to be translated into proteins, so this answer takes minutes to hours, not the seconds of the cAMP relay. (DNA is not drawn.)

cell.caption: Target genes on: new mRNA ×12 (drawn) in the nucleus.

sections.heading: A tree is built mostly from air
text: Follow the atoms of one glucose through one leaf cell. The chloroplast builds sugar from CO₂ and water using light energy; the mitochondrion of the same cell breaks sugar back to CO₂ to make ATP. Pick **Day** or **Night** to compare.

Simplified: one chloroplast and one mitochondrion drawn as plain ellipses; light reactions, the Calvin cycle and respiration are shown as summary steps; counts are per glucose; dry-mass shares are approximate. Sources: OpenStax Biology 2e ch. 7-8; Carbon TIME (MSU) plant mass ledger.

panels.title: Leaf cell · one glucose worth of atoms
panels.label: a leaf cell (cartoon)

initial.caption: Water arrives from the roots; CO₂ is in the air outside.

steps.text: An oak can weigh many tonnes, yet the soil it grew in has barely gone down. So where does a plant's mass come from? Follow the atoms in one leaf cell: water and minerals arrive from the roots, and CO₂ waits in the air outside.

ledger.note: Shares are of a plant's dry mass, approximate (Carbon TIME, MSU).

steps.text: Day. Chlorophyll in the chloroplast absorbs light, and water molecules enter the chloroplast. Light brings energy, not matter: no atom in the plant comes from sunlight.

cell.caption: Light is absorbed; 12 H₂O enter the chloroplast.

steps.text: Light reactions: water is split. Its oxygen pairs up as O₂, and its hydrogen and electrons are loaded onto NADPH while ATP is made. For one glucose: 12 H₂O give 6 O₂.

labels.text: every O in this O₂ came from water

cell.caption: Water split: O₂ forms; ATP and NADPH build up.

steps.text: The O₂ diffuses out of the cell into the air. The oxygen a plant gives off comes from water, not from CO₂, as isotope-labelling experiments showed.

cell.caption: 6 O₂ leave the leaf cell.

steps.text: CO₂ from the air diffuses into the cell and into the chloroplast. Six CO₂ carry the six carbon atoms that one glucose will need.

cell.caption: 6 CO₂ enter the chloroplast.

steps.text: Calvin cycle: an enzyme (rubisco) fixes the CO₂ onto an existing sugar, and the ATP and NADPH from the light reactions drive the rebuilding into new sugar. Six CO₂ make one 6-carbon sugar.

cell.caption: 6 CO₂ fixed into one sugar (6 C); ATP and NADPH spent.

ledger.note: Simplified: the Calvin cycle's product is a 3-carbon sugar, shown here as glucose.

steps.text: The sugar leaves the chloroplast. It becomes cellulose, starch and the other carbon compounds of the plant. The ledger answers the puzzle: about 96% of dry mass came from air and water; the soil gave only a few percent as minerals.

cell.caption: Sugar is the plant's building material.

ledger.note: Dry mass shares approximate (Carbon TIME, MSU). The rest of fresh mass is water.

steps.text: Plants respire too, in the same cell, day and night. Glycolysis in the cytoplasm splits one sugar (6 C) into two pyruvate (3 C each), for a net gain of 2 ATP. No carbon is lost yet.

cell.caption: Glycolysis: 1 sugar -> 2 pyruvate + 2 ATP.

steps.text: The pyruvate enters the mitochondrion. O₂ from the air diffuses in as well: it is needed at the very end of respiration.

cell.caption: Pyruvate and O₂ enter the mitochondrion.

steps.text: Inside, the pyruvate carbons leave as 6 CO₂ (link reaction and Krebs cycle). Their electrons pass down a transport chain to O₂, which becomes water, and the chain powers ATP synthase. Total: about 30-32 ATP per glucose, a textbook estimate.

cell.caption: 6 CO₂, 12 H₂O and about 30-32 ATP.

ledger.note: 12 H₂O form at the end of the chain; 6 water molecules are used up earlier in the Krebs cycle, so the net is 6 H₂O per glucose.

steps.text: The CO₂ diffuses back into the air: the same carbon atoms a leaf fixed can be fixed again. By day a leaf fixes far more CO₂ than it releases, so the plant grows.

cell.caption: 6 CO₂ back in the air: the loop closes.

steps.text: Night. With no light, water is not split, so no ATP or NADPH is made in the chloroplast, and the Calvin cycle stops too. CO₂ stays outside. The cell runs on sugar stored as starch during the day.

cell.caption: Dark: no light reactions, no CO₂ fixed.

ledger.note: Night path: photosynthesis stops; respiration continues.

log.text: dark: light reactions + Calvin cycle stop

steps.text: Respiration does not stop. Glycolysis splits the stored sugar, and the pyruvate and O₂ from the air enter the mitochondrion, exactly as by day.

cell.caption: Night: respiration continues.

steps.text: The mitochondrion releases CO₂, makes water from O₂ and makes about 30-32 ATP per glucose. With nothing fixing it, CO₂ outside builds up: at night a leaf is a net CO₂ source. Plants photosynthesise and respire, not one instead of the other.

labels.text: night: CO₂ out, none taken in

cell.caption: CO₂ outside: 6 -> 12. Nothing fixes it.

sections.heading: Own DNA versus foreign DNA
text: Bacteria are under constant pressure from DNA that is not their own. Many defend themselves with a restriction–modification system: a restriction enzyme that cuts DNA at one short recognition site, and a partner methylase that marks the same site on the bacterium's own DNA so it is left alone.

Follow the first path to see a foreign strand recognised, cut with a staggered cut and broken down. Switch to the second path to see why the identical site on the host chromosome survives. The sequence is illustrative and 24 letters long; real DNA molecules are thousands to millions of letters.

initial.caption: A double strand of DNA, drawn flat; the site GAATTC is boxed.
initial.note: Illustrative 24-letter sequence. Upper strand reads 5'→3' left to right; the lower strand pairs with it and runs the opposite way (3'→5').

steps.text: **Foreign DNA gets in.** A short piece of double-stranded DNA from outside has entered the bacterium. It is not part of the cell's own chromosome, and nothing in the cell has marked it.

scene.caption: A foreign double strand is now inside the cell.
scene.note: Illustrative sequence, not to scale. A real cell holds many copies of each enzyme drawn here.

steps.text: **The site is a palindrome.** Letters 9–14 read GAATTC on the upper strand, 5'→3'. Read the lower strand in its own 5'→3' direction (right to left) and it also spells GAATTC. The enzyme recognises exactly this six-letter pattern.

scene.caption: Both strands read GAATTC 5'→3': the site is a palindrome.
scene.note: Lower strand, letters 14 down to 9: G A A T T C. A six-letter site turns up by chance about once every 4,096 letters (4⁶) of random sequence.

steps.text: **The enzyme collides with the DNA and slides along it.** It holds the strand loosely and moves along it by random motion, checking letters, without cutting anything that does not match.

scene.caption: The enzyme binds loosely when it collides with the DNA, then slides.
scene.note: Dimmed letters have already been checked. Sliding is random back-and-forth motion, drawn here as a single pass to the right.

log.text: restriction enzyme slides along the DNA

steps.text: **It binds tightly at the site.** At GAATTC the shape of the DNA matches the enzyme's binding surface. The enzyme clamps on and grips both strands at once.

scene.caption: At GAATTC the enzyme grips both strands tightly.
scene.note: The enzyme works as a pair of identical halves, one for each strand. That matches the two-fold symmetry of the palindrome. Drawn here as one shape.

steps.text: **It cuts both backbones, offset by four letters.** The upper strand is cut between G and A, after letter 9. The lower strand is cut between letters 14 and 13, again just after G when read in its own 5'→3' direction. The two cuts are not opposite each other, so the cut is staggered.

scene.caption: Cut after G on each strand: upper between 9 and 10, lower between 13 and 14.
scene.note: Each strand is cut at G^AATTC, read in its own 5'→3' direction. The red marks show where the sugar-phosphate backbones were broken.

steps.text: **The pieces fall apart with sticky ends.** The four base pairs between the two cuts (AATT) are held only by weak hydrogen bonds, so they come apart. Each piece keeps four unpaired letters, an overhang. Both overhangs read AATT 5'→3', so they are complementary and can pair again.

scene.caption: Two pieces, each with a four-letter single-stranded overhang.
scene.note: Piece A: upper 1–9, lower 1–13. Piece B: upper 10–24, lower 14–24. Overhangs like these are called sticky ends.

steps.text: **The pieces are broken down.** Other nucleases in the cell attack the open ends and chop the fragments into single nucleotides. The cell reuses them, and the foreign DNA never gets to act. The restriction enzyme is unchanged and free to cut again.

scene.caption: A nuclease attacks the open ends of the pieces.
scene.note: Simplified: the nuclease is drawn on one piece only, and the breakdown itself is not animated. Like any enzyme, the restriction enzyme is not used up.

steps.text: **The bacterium's own DNA has the same site.** Its chromosome is long, so it carries GAATTC in many places, the same six letters the enzyme cuts. Something must stop the enzyme from cutting the cell's own genes.

scene.caption: The same six letters, now on the bacterium's own chromosome.
scene.note: Same illustrative letters as before, now standing for a short stretch of the host chromosome.

steps.text: **The methylase marks the site.** A partner enzyme recognises the same GAATTC. Instead of cutting, it adds a methyl group (CH₃) to one adenine on each strand: the second A of each GAATTC, counting from its 5' end. The letters do not change, but the site is now marked.

scene.caption: The methylase adds a methyl group to an A in the site.
scene.note: Methyl groups go on the upper A at 11 and the lower A at 12, drawn as one CH₃ marker. The methylase marks new sites soon after the chromosome is copied.

log.text: methylase adds CH₃ to the site

steps.text: **The restriction enzyme scans the host DNA.** It collides with the chromosome and slides along it exactly as before. Nothing about the enzyme has changed.

scene.caption: The same enzyme slides along the methylated host DNA.
scene.note: The methyl marker stays on the site after the methylase leaves.

log.text: restriction enzyme slides along host DNA

steps.text: **The methyl groups block binding.** The methyl groups stick into the groove where the enzyme needs close contact. The enzyme reaches GAATTC but cannot grip it tightly, so it does not cut.

scene.caption: The enzyme reaches the methylated site but cannot clamp on.
scene.note: Its state stays at 'binding' and never reaches 'bound'. No cut is made.

steps.text: **The host DNA stays whole.** The enzyme lets go and drifts off. Both backbones of the chromosome are unbroken. The same enzyme that destroyed the foreign strand leaves the cell's own DNA alone. The only difference is the methyl mark.

scene.caption: The enzyme leaves; both strands of the host DNA are intact.
scene.note: Compare with the foreign path: same letters, same enzyme, opposite outcome. Unmarked foreign DNA is cut; marked host DNA is spared.

sections.heading: Reading DNA in short pieces
text: A sequencer reads DNA by copying it one letter per cycle and recording each letter as it is added. Each read is short and a few letters are misread, so many overlapping reads are compared to decide what the sequence really is.

initial.note: Empty for now. Each finished read will be placed here, on the reference: a sequence already assembled for this species. A read goes where its letters match. A dot will mean the same letter as the reference, a red cell a different letter, and the grey bars above will show depth, the number of reads covering each position.

panels.title: Inside the sequencer, one cycle at a time
panels.label: top: template · bottom: copy, grows ←

initial.caption: Only the primer is paired. Offset letters = places not yet copied.

steps.text: **A fragment waits to be read.** The DNA has been broken into short single-stranded fragments. On this one a short primer of known sequence has paired near one end, leaving 16 unpaired letters beside it. The sequencer will build a matching copy along the template one letter at a time and record each letter as it is added.

log.text: fragment 1 → read 1: 16 cycles, one letter each

steps.text: **Cycle 1: one letter is added.** DNA polymerase adds the nucleotide that pairs with the next template letter (A with T, G with C). Every nucleotide offered carries a coloured tag that names its letter and a blocker that stops a second letter joining. A camera records the colour: the first letter is G.

dna.caption: Cycle 1: G pairs with C; its tag glows and is photographed

steps.text: **Cycle 2: unblock, then add one more.** After the picture, the tag and blocker are removed so the copy can take exactly one more letter. The copy grows from its 5' end toward its 3' end, which on this drawing is right to left. The second letter is A.
**Add, photograph, unblock, repeat.** Every cycle adds exactly one letter, so the cycle number is the letter's position in the read. After eight cycles the read so far is GATTACAG.

**After 16 cycles the run stops.** Read 1 is 16 letters long; the last two template letters on the left are never read. Real instruments photograph clusters of many identical copies at once. In late cycles some copies fall out of step, so errors become more common toward the end of a read.

dna.caption: Cycle 16: read complete; template letters 1–2 not read

steps.text: **The read is found on the reference.** A reference is a sequence already assembled for the species. Read 1 matches positions 12,401–12,416 letter for letter; a dot means "same letter as the reference". The map shows this stretch lies inside gene A.

dna.caption: Read 1 is finished. Next: find where it sits on the reference.

pile.note: Dot = same letter as the reference.

steps.text: **Millions of fragments are read side by side.** The DNA came from many cells, so other fragments cover the same stretch, each starting at a different place. Their reads overlap read 1 and stack up on the reference.

dna.caption: Other fragments, read the same way, give reads 2–5.

steps.text: **Five reads now cover the middle.** The grey bars above the reference show depth: how many reads cover each position. Two letters disagree with the reference, at 12,415 and at 12,419. Is each one a real difference, or a misread?

pile.note: Grey bars = depth. Red cell = differs from the reference.

steps.text: **A real difference: two of five reads say A.** At 12,415 the reference has G; reads 2 and 4 carry A and the other three carry G. Most body cells carry two copies of each chromosome, one from each parent. A steady split like this between independent reads is the sign that the two copies differ at this letter (a heterozygous site). With only five reads this is a teaching example; real calls use many more.

log.text: 12,415: G in 3 reads, A in 2 → real difference

steps.text: **A likely error: one read alone.** At 12,419 only read 2 shows T; the three other reads covering it agree with the reference C. It is also read 2's last letter, where errors are most common. One disagreeing letter among agreeing reads is treated as a misread, not a real difference.

log.text: 12,419: T in 1 of 4 reads → likely misread

steps.text: **Many imperfect reads make one confident sequence.** No single read is trusted on its own. Where reads overlap, agreement confirms a letter, a steady split reveals a real difference, and a lone mismatch is set aside. Real studies collect far more reads per position than five (often 30 or more); this pile is classroom sized.

pile.note: Real piles are far deeper than five reads.

steps.text: **Alternate ending: only two reads cover the site.** Fragments come from random places, so some stretches get few reads. Here only reads 1 and 2 came from this stretch, and depth at 12,415 is just 2.

**No confident call.** One read says G and one says A. That could be two different chromosome copies, or a single misread letter; two reads cannot tell these apart. The honest answer is "unknown here" until more reads are collected.
